name: Novice/non-native authorial disclaimer
instruction: Check the story's margins (opening or closing notes) for an explicit hedge about the author's own competence: an apology for language errors, a statement that English isn't their first language, or a statement that this is an early or first attempt at creative writing. HIGH: such a disclaimer is present anywhere in the text. LOW: no authorial competence disclaimer appears.

name: Tonal Control
instruction: Score high when humor, horror, sentiment, or absurdity are balanced deliberately and shifts reinforce the story’s premise; score low when tonal changes feel accidental or undermine the emotional effect.

name: External audience footprint
instruction: Count named subreddits, personal archives, linked catalogs, invitations to read more work, and recognizable author branding; high means the story carries several routes into an existing audience, while low means no external destination or brand appears.

name: Body-part and sensory word count
instruction: Count how many times the story uses the words 'hand', 'hands', 'eye', 'eyes', 'breath', 'skin', 'blood', 'throat', 'chest'. Score 1.0 for many occurrences, 0.5 for a few, 0.0 for none. Count the listed words only; pay no attention to whether the physical writing is effective.

name: Economy of Explanation
instruction: Score high when the story conveys necessary context through selected details and lets readers infer the rest; score low when it pauses for redundant exposition, technical listing, or explanation that the scene does not need.

name: Sustained, distinctive narrating voice
instruction: Judge whether the narration maintains one deliberate, recognizable register (specific diction, syntax, and tone appropriate to who is narrating) consistently across the whole piece, versus drifting into a flat, generic, or inconsistent register that could belong to any narrator. HIGH: you could identify this piece from a blind paragraph because of its voice. LOW: the prose reads as interchangeable default 'competent internet fiction' voice, or shifts registers without motivation.

name: Embodied Scene Presence
instruction: Score high when setting and emotion are conveyed through specific sensory perceptions, physical behavior, and concrete objects; score low when the story relies mainly on summary or abstract explanation.

name: Reader-facing boilerplate
instruction: Count author notes, thanks, edit apologies, feedback requests, and generic promotional closers. High means several such elements; low means none or nearly none.

name: Emotional payoff earned by prior stakes-building
instruction: Judge whether the story establishes enough context, character investment, or concrete stakes before asserting a major emotional beat (a death, a danger, a revelation), such that the beat feels dramatized rather than merely announced. HIGH: by the time the emotional claim arrives, the reader has been given real material to feel it with. LOW: a large emotional claim is asserted (stated as fact) without the scene-work needed to make a reader feel its weight.

name: Prompt enacted through consequence, not recited
instruction: Score 5 when the prompt's proposition is demonstrated by events and their costs, such that the story would still work if the prompt's sentence were never spoken aloud in it. Score 1 when the prompt's sentence (or a close paraphrase) is itself the payoff, or when the story is a tableau of the prompt plus backstory explaining how the tableau came about. Restating the prompt early as a scene-setter is neutral; restating it as the climax is the low end.

name: Earned idea payoff from the premise
instruction: Score 5 when the story works out a genuine implication of its own premise that the reader was not handed -- a mechanism, a paradox, a social logic, an inverted consequence -- and the working-out is legible in the text. Score 1 when the premise is illustrated but never interrogated, so the story ends knowing exactly what it knew at the start.

name: Copy-editing regularity
instruction: Assess consistency of spelling, grammar, punctuation, paragraph spacing, and typographic conventions; high means few visible errors and stable formatting, while low means repeated slips or inconsistent mechanics.

name: Diction precision and internal consistency
instruction: Judge whether word choices are used correctly and consistently, and whether small factual/continuity details (spelling of body parts, repeated invented terms) are handled with control, distinguishing genuine precision from small slips a careful editor would flag. HIGH: word choices are exact and repeatable details stay consistent. LOW: there is a word-choice error (a wrong word used for its sound rather than meaning) or a repeated but unclear/misused term.

name: Serial-instalment furniture and pre-assumed world lore
instruction: Count two things. (a) Explicit instalment markers: a series or book title above the prose, part/chapter numbering, 'Previous Chapter' or 'First Chapter' links, a note that this continues or accompanies other pieces. (b) Proper nouns for people, factions, wars, gods or places that are used without any in-text introduction, as if the reader already knows them. HIGH = a chapter header with back-links plus five or more unglossed proper nouns in the first 300 words. LOW = a self-contained piece in which every named entity is introduced in scene. Count the markers and the names; do not judge whether the worldbuilding is good or bad.

name: Earned Payoff
instruction: Score high when the ending delivers a consequence or reversal prepared by earlier details and changes the reader’s understanding; score low when it is arbitrary, merely announced, or absent.

name: The story refuses to gloss itself
instruction: Score 5 when the emotional point and the joke are both left for the reader to complete, so the last line performs rather than summarizes. Score 1 when the text states its own meaning, names the feeling it has just produced, or explains its own punchline. Ignore whether the meaning is obvious; score only whether the story says it out loud.

name: Markdown vertical-whitespace density
instruction: Count paragraph breaks that use extra blank lines or trailing double-space line-break formatting, producing unusually large vertical gaps between short lines or single sentences. HIGH: most paragraphs/lines are separated by two or more blank lines, or single sentences sit isolated with wide gaps around them (an airy, staccato page layout). LOW: standard single-blank-line paragraph breaks with ordinary multi-sentence paragraphs and no excess white space.

name: Transcript or log format
instruction: Count role labels, timestamps, chat-style turns, and other transcript conventions. High means the story is substantially presented as a log or exchange; low means conventional prose narration.

name: Form That Serves Content
instruction: Score high when the chosen form—poem, log, transcript, dialogue, or other structure—creates meaning, pacing, or limitations essential to the story; score low when formatting is merely decorative or the form could be removed without loss.

name: Self-contained: no borrowed affect from outside the text
instruction: Score 5 when all emotional weight is generated inside the shown text, so a reader with no outside knowledge gets the full effect. Score 1 when the story leans on an existing franchise, an earlier installment, or thread context to supply the feeling or the recognition, and a reader lacking that context loses the point. Note the exception: if the prompt itself names the borrowed material, borrowing is licensed and only the failure to add anything to it counts against the story.

name: Causal Escalation
instruction: Score high when each major beat changes the characters’ options and increases pressure toward a consequential climax; score low when events remain static, arrive abruptly, or merely accumulate without changing the situation.

name: First-person pronoun count
instruction: Count how heavily the story uses the first-person singular pronouns 'I', 'me', 'my', 'mine'. Score 1.0 when they appear very frequently throughout, 0.5 when they appear occasionally, 0.0 when they are absent or near-absent. Count the pronouns only; pay no attention to whether the narration is any good.

name: Dynamic Power in Relationships
instruction: Score high when dialogue and action reveal changing leverage, mismatched knowledge, dependence, affection, or threat between characters; score low when interactions merely exchange exposition and leave the relationships unchanged.

name: Distinctiveness of central conceit
instruction: Judge whether the story's core idea offers a genuinely surprising angle, combination, or reversal on its prompt, versus executing a familiar genre convention straightforwardly with no distinguishing hook. HIGH: the central idea is one you haven't seen many times before, or combines familiar elements in an unexpected way. LOW: the premise is a stock genre setup (a quest, a diplomatic incident, a fated meeting) executed competently but without any distinguishing twist on the idea itself.

name: Contest-compliance furniture: word counts and organizer address
instruction: Count artifacts that show the piece was submitted into a structured event rather than posted freely: an explicit numeric word count, a round or heat identifier, a note addressed to organizers or to fellow entrants, an off-topic aside to the person who supplied the stimulus. HIGH = an explicit numeric word count or round identifier together with an address to the running of the event. MEDIUM = one such artifact alone. LOW = nothing addressed to anyone except the reader of the story.
